persona.brief_background: María structures her evenings around winding down with a well-crafted mystery or procedural — she times her knitting rows to scene breaks and often annotates plot points in the margins of her reading journal. She prioritizes community involvement (runs a weekly book club at the local library) and uses crime shows as a social bridge, recommending series to colleagues and bringing plot discussions into classroom reading activities.

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, approachable and quietly authoritative — the voice of a caring teacher-librarian who enjoys friendly literary debate. Moderately formal in professional contexts but conversational and wry with colleagues and community members; shares clear, actionable recommendations and personal anecdotes to build rapport.
general_writing_style.syntax: Prefers clear declarative and compound sentences with occasional subordinate clauses for nuance; uses brief parenthetical asides and commas for friendly asides. Often poses rhetorical questions to engage readers and strings short clauses for checklist-style recommendations rather than long, ornate sentences.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Draws on library and literary vocabulary: words like 'catalog', 'circulation', 'hold request', 'interlibrary loan', 'ISBN', and genre labels such as 'cozy mystery', 'procedural', 'red herring' and 'narrative arc'. Also uses hobby-specific terms ('row', 'purl', 'cast on'; baking terms like 'proof', 'crumb', 'glaze'), everyday US measurements ('cups', 'degrees F'), and occasional Spanish phrases for warmth (e.g., '¿qué tal?', 'mi gente', '¡qué buen giro!').
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of contractions ('I'm', 'can't', 'we'll') and parenthetical asides ('(I time my knitting to scene breaks)'). Habitually invites participation with phrases and questions like 'Have you read...?', 'check it out', 'hold a copy', and uses community-oriented 'we' plus occasional regional or Spanish interjections such as 'y'all', 'oye' and 'claro'.

contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Warm, reassuring and plainly informative with a caring teacher-librarian voice. Moderately formal phrasing for clarity, softened by a personal aside and an invitation to follow up by phone or in person.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Use gentle openings and sign-offs, occasional Spanish warmth, and clear action steps in short sentences. Examples: "Thank you for reaching out," "I recommend we...," "¿qué tal if we..." Use parenthetical asides for context (e.g., "(she enjoys mysteries)") and rhetorical questions to invite engagement: "Would you like me to hold a copy?" Keep sentences declarative and concise: "I'll place it on hold and notify you."

task_instruction: Send an overdue book reminder to a parent.
task_details: Student Mateo Rivera, 3rd grade, has an overdue book titled 'The Case of the Missing Cupcake' (call number MYS RIV). The book was due 10 days ago. Explain the overdue policy, offer options (renew, return, or replace), and invite the parent to contact the library or stop by. Include a gentle tone and a follow-up action: librarian will hold a copy if requested.
personalized:
Hello Mrs. Rivera,

Thank you for everything you do to support Mateo's reading. I'm writing because Mateo's copy of 'The Case of the Missing Cupcake' (call number MYS RIV) is 10 days overdue. Our circulation policy asks families to either return, renew, or replace items so other students can enjoy them too.

Would you like me to renew it for another week? If you'd prefer, I can place a replacement hold and notify you when the new copy arrives (I'll hold it for Mateo). If the book is lost, our replacement cost is $12, but we can work something out—just let me know.

Please call the library at 916-555-0123 or reply to this email and tell me what you'd like to do. ¿Qué tal if we plan to have Mateo bring it in by Friday? If that's not possible, we'll find another solution.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian
(Feel free to stop by after school or call; I'm happy to help.)

task_instruction: Notify a parent about a damaged book returned and outline next steps.
task_details: Student Sofia Nguyen, 2nd grade, returned 'National Geographic Kids: Ocean' with water damage and a torn page. Describe condition, mention repair vs. replacement options, list estimated repair cost $6 and replacement cost $18, and request parent's decision within one week. Offer to discuss by phone or in person.
personalized:
Dear Ms. Nguyen,

Thank you for bringing Sofia's book back to the library. When she returned 'National Geographic Kids: Ocean' we noticed water damage and one torn page that affects the pictures. We can attempt a professional repair (estimated $6) or replace the copy (replacement cost $18).

Could you let me know which option you'd prefer within a week? If you'd like to discuss payment plans or alternatives, I'm happy to talk by phone or meet briefly after drop-off. We want to keep Sofia reading (she loves nonfiction) and keep our collection in good shape for all students.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian
916-555-0123 (call anytime during library hours)

task_instruction: Recommend mystery books for a student who enjoys mysteries.
task_details: Parent of 5th grader Liam O'Connor asked for age-appropriate mystery recommendations. Liam likes Sherlock-style puzzles and likes series with recurring detective kids. Provide three specific title recommendations with brief reasons, offer to place holds, and invite the parent to reply or call.
personalized:
Hello Mr. O'Connor,

Thanks for asking about books for Liam. He mentioned he enjoys Sherlock-style puzzles, so I have three suggestions I think he'll like. 'The Great Greene Heist' by Varian Johnson has clever twists and a strong team dynamic (good for readers who like problem-solving). 'Encyclopedia Brown, Boy Detective' is classic short mysteries he can digest in one sitting (perfect for knitting-row breaks—okay, I mean quick reads). 'The Mysterious Benedict Society' has a smart puzzle arc and recurring characters he can follow.

Would you like me to place any of these on hold for Liam? I can hold them at the circulation desk and text you when they arrive. Reply to this email or call 916-555-0123 and tell me which titles to hold.

¿Qué tal if we start with one from each style and see which he prefers? I'm happy to fine-tune the list after he reads a few.

Warmly,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Request parental permission for a student's participation in an online summer reading program.
task_details: 4th grader Aisha Khan is interested in the district summer reading program which requires parent consent to set up an online account (name, grade, and parent email needed). Explain program benefits, privacy safeguards, what information is collected, and include a yes/no reply request. Offer to set up account at school if parent prefers.
personalized:
Dear Mrs. Khan,

Thank you for encouraging Aisha's reading this summer. Aisha is signed up for our district summer reading program, which includes an online account so she can log books, earn badges, and join virtual storytimes. To create the account I need your permission to use Aisha's name, grade, and your email address. The program only collects basic information and follows district privacy guidelines (no student data is shared publicly).

Would you like me to create the account for Aisha? Reply 'yes' with the preferred email address, or tell me if you'd rather I set it up in person at the library. If you prefer not to participate online, Aisha can still join the in-person activities and earn prizes.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian
(You can call me at 916-555-0123 if you have questions about privacy.)

task_instruction: Inform a parent that a student returned a book late and it was reshelved without check-in; explain hold process.
task_details: 5th grader Daniel Morales returned 'Framed!' late and left it on the cart; it was reshelved before being checked in, affecting a hold for another student. Explain how holds work, apologize for the confusion, and offer to place a new hold and waive the overdue fine as a courtesy. Invite the parent to contact the librarian if they prefer another arrangement.
personalized:
Hello Mr. Morales,

Thank you for returning Daniel's book 'Framed!'. I wanted to let you know the book was put back on the shelf before it was officially checked in, and that temporarily delayed a hold for another student. I'm sorry for the mix-up (we try to avoid that!).

To make things right, I'll place a new hold for the other student and waive any overdue fines for Daniel's account as a courtesy. If you'd like me to remind Daniel to bring checked-out books to the circulation desk in the future, I'm happy to do so gently at check-out.

Would that work for you? Call or reply and I'll take care of it.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Advise a parent whose child selected a book with mature themes and propose alternatives.
task_details: Parent of 5th grader Emma Davis is concerned Emma checked out 'A Certain Shadow' which contains brief references to family loss. Acknowledge parent's concern, describe observation about the content, suggest three age-appropriate alternatives addressing similar themes gently, offer to remove the book from Emma's account and place alternatives on hold, invite meeting or phone call.
personalized:
Dear Ms. Davis,

Thank you for reaching out. I understand your concern about Emma's copy of 'A Certain Shadow' and its references to family loss. I reviewed the book and agree it has a few scenes that might be more suited to older readers.

If you'd like, I can remove the book from Emma's account and recommend gentler titles that still explore feelings and resilience. 'Bridge to Terabithia' handles grief in a sensitive way, 'Tuck Everlasting' looks at life choices with a soft touch, and 'Because of Winn-Dixie' shows healing through community (all appropriate for 5th grade). I can place any of these on hold and notify you.

Would you like me to swap the book now? I'm available to talk by phone or meet briefly at pick-up if you'd prefer a quick conversation.

Warmly,
María López
Elementary School Librarian
916-555-0123

task_instruction: Notify a parent that a requested hold is ready for pickup.
task_details: Parent Ms. Johnson requested two books for her 3rd grader Olivia: 'Pax' and 'The Wild Robot'. Notify that both are ready at the circulation desk for pick-up within 5 school days. Include hours, mention hold will be released after 5 days, offer to extend if needed, and sign off warmly.
personalized:
Hello Ms. Johnson,

Good news—Olivia's holds ('Pax' and 'The Wild Robot') are ready for pickup at the circulation desk. They will be held for five school days and then released to the next patron, so please stop by within that window.

Our library hours are 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM on weekdays. Would you like me to extend the hold if you need more time? Just reply or call and I'll take care of it.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian
(We love seeing families come in together—bring Olivia by and we'll show her other suggestions she might like.)

task_instruction: Explain interlibrary loan arrival and pick-up details to a parent.
task_details: 4th grader Noah Patel requested 'Wonder' via interlibrary loan. Book is expected to arrive in two weeks. Explain how interlibrary loan works, mention no charge, that the book must be returned by a specific date (two weeks after pick-up), and request parent to notify librarian if they prefer to cancel. Offer to place a local copy hold instead if they prefer quicker access.
personalized:
Dear Mr. Patel,

I wanted to update you about Noah's request for 'Wonder'. We placed an interlibrary loan for the title and expect it to arrive in about two weeks. Interlibrary loan lets us borrow from other libraries when we don't have a copy on our shelves; there is no charge for you.

Once it arrives, the lending library usually asks for a two-week loan period, so we will need the book returned by the due date noted on the slip. If you'd rather not wait, I can place a local hold on any nearby branch copy (sometimes faster) and notify you.

Please let me know if you'd like me to cancel the interlibrary loan and try the local hold instead.

Warmly,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Send a summer reading suggestions email tailored to a 1st grader.

Provide a short list of picture books and early readers (5 titles), include a note about reading aloud, 15-minute daily goal, and offer to prepare a small take-home packet from the library. personalized:
Hola Señora Martinez,

Summer is a great time to keep Isabella reading a little each day. Here are five gentle choices she might enjoy: 'Frog and Toad Are Friends' by Arnold Lobel, 'A Chair for My Mother' by Vera B. Williams, 'Press Here' by Hervé Tullet, 'Henry and Mudge' by Cynthia Rylant, and 'Last Stop on Market Street' by Matt de la Peña. Reading aloud together for 15 minutes a day keeps fluency and confidence strong (and it's a lovely habit).

Would you like me to prepare a small take-home packet with one picture book and two early readers for Isabella to pick up before the last day of school? Reply and I'll set them aside.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Respond to a parent's request to change their child's reading level placement.
task_details: Parent of 2nd grader Jacob Smith feels his current guided reading level is too easy. personalized:
Hello Mr. Smith,

Thank you for sharing your thoughts about Jacob's reading level. We base guided reading placement on classroom observations and occasional assessments, but we also adjust when a child shows readiness.

¿Qué tal if we try a trial set of slightly higher-level books for one week and see how Jacob manages? I'll select three titles that stretch his skills without causing frustration and check in with you after a week. Of course, we can change course anytime based on how he responds.

Would you like me to set those aside for Jacob?

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_details: Student Carlos Ruiz, 4th grade, was observed running in the library and shouting during library time, disrupting others. personalized:
Dear Mr. Ruiz,

I wanted to let you know about a behaviour we noticed from Carlos today. During library time he was running and shouting, which disrupted other students who were reading. We spoke with him briefly and reminded him of our library expectations for quiet and respect.

To support Carlos, I suggest a one-week behaviour plan: I will give gentle verbal reminders and, if needed, a quiet timeout in the office area. We'll also offer positive reinforcement when he follows the rules. Would you be willing to support this plan at home? I'm happy to meet or talk by phone to make sure we present a consistent message.

Gracias for partnering with us.
María López
Elementary School Librarian

We're putting together our spring library newsletter and would love to include a photo of Ana holding her favorite book from storytime. We respect family privacy and can either include no name, only Ana's first name and grade, or no identifying information at all.

Would you be comfortable with us using Ana's photo? Reply 'yes' with your preference (no name, first name only, or no ID). If you'd rather not, that's absolutely fine—just tell me and we'll keep her out of the pictures.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

Would you like me to email you the reconsideration form or set up a short meeting to talk this through?

Gracias,
María López

Hola Señora García,

Qué gusto que Rosa is reading in both Spanish and English. Here are five bilingual picture books I recommend: 'My Many Colored Days' (simple emotions in both languages), 'Last Stop on Market Street' (beautiful rhythm and community themes), 'Round Is a Tortilla' (great for discussing shapes and culture), 'Abuela' (family connection and gentle bilingual text), and 'Sing, Don't Cry' (short, lyrical, good for read-aloud).

Would you like me to place any of these on hold for you to pick up? I can also recommend authors to read aloud at home or at our next bilingual storytime.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

Dear Mrs. Brown,

Thank you for meeting about Ethan's screening. I know hearing that can feel concerning, and I want you to know we're here to support him. Based on the screening, focused phonics practice will help. At school we can offer phonics flashcards, guided reading groups, and leveled readers targeted to his needs.

At home, a short 15-minute phonics practice, daily read-aloud, and simple sounding-out games can make a big difference. Would you like to schedule a weekly 20-minute reading time at the library with me? I can also connect you with our district reading specialist if you'd like more intensive support.

Warmly,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Recommend books for a reluctant reader and offer to place them on hold.
task_details: Parent Ms. Blake concerns about her 4th grader Noah being a reluctant reader. Suggest five engaging, low-pressure titles (series and standalones) with brief reasons (short chapters, humor, illustrations), offer to place two on hold, and invite parent to a quick meeting to discuss reading strategies.
personalized:
Hello Ms. Blake,

Thanks for telling me about Noah. For reluctant readers I often start with books that are fast-paced, funny, or heavily illustrated. Try 'Dog Man' (comic format, silly and readable), 'Nate the Great' (short mysteries), 'The Last Kids on Earth' (action and humor), 'Ivy + Bean' (relatable friendship stories), and 'The Bad Guys' (graphic-novel-style chapters).

Would you like me to place two of these on hold for Noah? I'm also happy to meet for 10 minutes to share gentle strategies to make reading feel like play rather than work.

Gracias,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

Dear Mrs. Perez,

I'm sorry I missed our scheduled meeting about Mateo's reading plan this afternoon. An unexpected assembly required my presence. I apologize for any inconvenience.

Would any of these times work for you next week: Monday at 3:30 PM, Wednesday at 8:15 AM, or Thursday at 4:00 PM? We can meet in person or connect by phone if that's easier. I remain committed to supporting Mateo and will come prepared with a short plan and book suggestions.

Gracias for your understanding,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Propose adding a focused mystery and historical-fiction circulating collection
task_details: Write an email to the principal proposing a new coordinated collection of age-appropriate mystery and historical-fiction titles for grades 3–5. Include rationale referencing circulation trends showing increased student holds, curriculum alignment with social studies units, a proposed budget estimate ($1,200), and a suggested timeline for selection and cataloging. Close with a request to meet for 20 minutes to review a preliminary title list.
personalized:
Dear Principal Rivera,

I'm writing to propose that we expand the library's circulating collection with a focused set of age-appropriate mystery and historical-fiction titles for grades 3–5. Because our circulation data shows a steady rise in mystery holds and frequent requests for historical stories during social studies units, this expansion would support curriculum alignment and sustain student engagement during unit studies. I estimate the initial purchase would be approximately $1,200, which would cover 60–80 paperback and hardcover copies chosen for reading-level breadth and durability, and I would coordinate cataloging and processing so titles are ready within six weeks. Could we schedule 20 minutes next week to review a preliminary title list and budget breakdown?

Gracias y saludos,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Request funding for an audiobook subscription service
task_details: Compose an email asking the principal to fund an audiobook subscription (e.g., OverDrive/Libby or similar) to increase equitable access for students who benefit from audio formats. Include evidence-based benefits for struggling readers and multilingual learners, a projected annual cost ($900), and a plan for integrating audiobooks into classroom reading plans and holds. End by proposing a 20-minute meeting to discuss implementation and licensing considerations.
personalized:
Dear Principal Johnson,

I'm writing to propose that we subscribe to an audiobook platform such as OverDrive/Libby to support students who benefit from audio formats, including our struggling readers and multilingual learners. Research and our experience show that audiobooks improve comprehension and vocabulary acquisition when paired with text, and because our hold request logs include frequent audiobook inquiries, this subscription would increase equitable access and reduce wait times. The projected annual cost is approximately $900 for a school-level collection, and I would work with teachers to integrate audiobooks into guided reading and classroom reading plans. Could we schedule 20 minutes to discuss licensing options and a rollout timeline?

Warmly,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Propose a bilingual Spanish-English picture book collection
task_details: Draft an email requesting approval and funding to purchase a bilingual Spanish-English picture book collection for K–2 family check-out. Mention demographic needs, support for dual-language development, an estimated cost ($800), and a plan to tag holdings with bilingual subject headings in the catalog. Conclude with a meeting proposal for 15–20 minutes to go over sample titles and labeling.
personalized:
Dear Principal Martinez,

I'm writing to propose that we add a curated bilingual Spanish-English picture book collection for K–2 that families can check out for home reading. Because our community includes many Spanish-speaking households and dual-language development is crucial in early literacy, this collection would support home-school connections and improve emergent literacy skills, and I would tag each title with clear bilingual subject headings in our catalog for easy holds and discovery. The estimated start-up cost is about $800 and I will coordinate with parent volunteers for translation-friendly caregiver guides. Could we schedule 20 minutes this month to look at sample titles and discuss labeling and cataloging?

Muchas gracias,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Request funds for flexible seating and reading nooks renovation
task_details: Write an email proposing minor renovations in the library to create flexible seating and cozy reading nooks to increase circulation and on-site reading time. Include evidence that comfortable spaces improve reading engagement, a proposed budget ($1,500), safety and ADA considerations, and a phased plan for installation over the summer. Dear Principal Allen,

I'm writing to propose a modest renovation of our library to add flexible seating and cozy reading nooks, which would create welcoming spaces that encourage longer on-site reading and higher circulation. Because studies and our observations show that comfortable, accessible spaces increase student engagement and library utilization, I propose a $1,500 budget for commercial-grade bean chairs, low shelving to create alcoves, and ADA-compliant seating, and I will ensure all items meet safety standards. I suggest we phase installation over the summer to avoid disruption, and I will provide floor plans and vendor quotes. Could we schedule 20 minutes next week to review options and timelines?

Kind regards,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

Dear Principal Brooks,

I'm writing to propose purchasing leveled literacy intervention kits for K–2 that include manipulatives, decodable texts, and teacher guides to support guided reading interventions. Sincerely,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

I'm writing to propose a summer reading incentive program in partnership with our local bookstore and public library branch to help reduce summer slide and maintain reading momentum. I will manage outreach and coordinate with partners to promote the program to families. Could we schedule 20 minutes to discuss partnership agreements and promotional strategies?

Warmly,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

I'm writing to propose purchasing classroom sets of three grade-appropriate novels to align with our 5th-grade literature circle curriculum. I will provide ISBNs and suggested lesson ties for each title. Could we schedule 20 minutes to review the selected titles and budget?

Sincerely,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

María López

Dear Principal Williams,

I'm writing to propose creating a sensory-friendly reading area in the library with soft lighting, noise-dampening panels, and curated sensory-friendly books and props to better serve our neurodiverse students. Could we schedule 20 minutes to review a proposed design and procurement plan?

Kind regards,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

I'm writing to propose that we increase the library's interlibrary loan budget to reduce wait times for high-demand titles that students and teachers request. Could we schedule 20 minutes this week to discuss policy adjustments and tracking methods?

Sincerely,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Lead with a brief purpose statement, follow with two to three short supporting sentences, and end with a specific request or meeting proposal. Examples: "I'm writing to propose...", "This supports our literacy goals by...", "Could we schedule 20 minutes to discuss?" Use compound sentences with subordinate clauses for nuance: "Because our circulation data shows..., I propose..." Avoid slang; use professional terms like "circulation," "hold request," and "curriculum alignment."

task_instruction: Request funds for Spanish-language family story kits for check-out
task_details: Write an email requesting funding ($400) to create family story kits in Spanish that can be checked out and used at home. Include contents (picture books, activity cards, vocabulary lists), alignment with family literacy goals, and cataloging plans with clear bilingual labels. End with a 20-minute meeting request to review proposed titles and kit contents.
personalized:
Dear Principal Soto,

I'm writing to propose creating family story kits in Spanish for home check-out that include picture books, activity cards, and simple vocabulary lists to support shared reading at home. Because family-centered materials strengthen home literacy routines and reflect our community's needs, I propose a $400 budget to assemble 30 kits with bilingual labeling and catalog entries that make holds simple for caregivers. I will provide usage guidance in English and Spanish. Could we schedule 20 minutes to review proposed titles and kit contents?

Muchas gracias,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, approachable and quietly authoritative — the voice of a caring teacher-librarian who enjoys friendly literary debate. general_writing_style.syntax: Prefers clear declarative and compound sentences with occasional subordinate clauses for nuance; uses brief parenthetical asides and commas for friendly asides. general_writing_style.lexicon: Draws on library and literary vocabulary: words like 'catalog', 'circulation', 'hold request', 'interlibrary loan', 'ISBN', and genre labels such as 'cozy mystery', 'procedural', 'red herring' and 'narrative arc'. general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of contractions ('I'm', 'can't', 'we'll') and parenthetical asides ('(I time my knitting to scene breaks)'). Habitually invites participation with phrases and questions like 'Have you read...?', 'check it out', 'hold a copy', and uses community-oriented 'we' plus occasional regional or Spanish interjections such as 'y'all', 'oye' and 'claro'.

task_instruction: Propose a cross-grade mystery-writing workshop culminating in a student anthology
task_details: Compose an email proposing a cross-grade (grades 4–6) mystery-writing workshop series led by the librarian that culminates in a printed anthology of student stories. Include learning objectives, estimated printing costs ($350), schedule (six weekly sessions), and plans for teacher collaboration and publication permissions. Request a 20-minute meeting to finalize timeline and budget.
personalized:
Dear Principal Vega,

I'm writing to propose a cross-grade mystery-writing workshop series for grades 4–6 that would culminate in a printed anthology of student stories. Because focused writing workshops develop narrative structure, red herrings, and revision skills, the series would meet weekly for six sessions, include teacher collaboration for in-class drafts, and cost approximately $350 to print anthologies for participants and the school library. I will secure parental publication permissions and manage the editorial process. Could we schedule 20 minutes to finalize the timeline and budget?

Sincerely,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Propose a literacy-focused 'escape room' event for reading comprehension
task_details: Write an email proposing a library-based literacy escape-room event tied to comprehension and critical thinking for grades 4–6, describing learning outcomes, staffing needs, materials budget ($200), and scheduling during a school event or evening. personalized:
Dear Principal King,

I'm writing to propose hosting a literacy-themed escape-room event in the library for grades 4–6 that uses reading comprehension and critical thinking puzzles to unlock successive clues. Because interactive challenges teach close reading, inference, and collaboration, this event would align with curriculum goals and run during an evening school event or a special school day, and I estimate $200 for materials and props, with staff and volunteer oversight to ensure safety and accessibility. I will design puzzles at multiple reading levels so all students can participate. Could we schedule 20 minutes to discuss dates, staffing, and safety considerations?

Saludos cordiales,

María López
Elementary School Librarian

Warmly,

María López

I'm writing to propose expanding our volunteer storytime program by recruiting and training parent volunteers, and to request modest funding to cover background check fees for volunteers who need support. María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_instruction: Plan a mystery-themed reading week for third graders linking to local history
task_details: Third grade cross-curricular week combining mystery picture books with local history. Goal is to build inference skills and civic awareness over five library visits in a two-week span. Library to provide read-alouds, three picture book titles, detective notebooks for students, and a short culminating class presentation. Teacher to align morning meeting prompts and one social studies mini-lesson. Schedule visit dates and share responsibilities; order two extra copies if possible.
personalized:
Hi Ana,

¿qué tal? I'd love to team up on a mystery-themed reading week that ties into our local history unit for third grade. My idea: five short library visits across two weeks where we build inference skills with picture-book mysteries and a focus on community places. I can bring three picture books (I was thinking a gentle town mystery, a historical mystery picture book, and a bilingual title), create detective notebooks for each student, and run the read-alouds and a short inference mini-lesson (I can cover circulation that week). Would you be open to doing a morning-meeting prompt on clue-gathering each day and teaching a 10-minute social studies connection to the place featured in the story?

Logistics we should confirm: visit dates that work for your class, I can order two extra copies if we want small-group reads (budget permitting), and I'll prepare a one-page family note so students can share the project at home. What do you think about starting the week of the 15th? I can draft the schedule and drop it in your mailbox (or email it), and I already have a stack of detective notebooks we can personalize.

Looking forward to scheming — in the friendliest, most librarian way possible. Would you like me to bring a scarf and a magnifying glass for dramatic effect? (I knit while I read, so expect calm energy.)

Abrazos, María

task_details: Fourth grade ELA lesson where students analyze procedural texts and then write their own short how-to instructions in the voice of a detective creating clues. One 45-minute library co-teach session for modeling and mentor texts, one follow-up 30-minute classroom workshop. Librarian provides mentor procedural texts, graphic organizer, and formative checklist. Teacher to plan rubric alignment and lead revision session. Target week: next month.
personalized:
Hola Miguel,

Let’s try a hands-on procedural writing lesson where fourth graders study procedural texts and then write a short how-to in the voice of a detective — basically instructions that could guide a fellow sleuth through a clue. I can bring mentor texts that show clear steps and vivid verbs, a simple graphic organizer, and a formative checklist we can use for peer review (I’ll handle photocopies and circulation that week). Would you be willing to plan the rubric criteria with me so we’re aligned on success, and lead the classroom revision session after students draft? I imagine two chunks: a 45-minute co-teach modeling and mentor-text read-aloud in the library, then a 30-minute follow-up workshop in your room.

Concrete asks: pick a week next month that works, tell me the number of students, and any IEP accommodations to note. I’ll prep mentor texts and bring pencils and sticky notes for peer feedback. Sound good? Want me to time my knitting rows to the lesson plan for dramatic effect? (Just kidding — mostly.)

Gracias, María

Librarian to contact author, arrange tech or room, gather student questions, and provide five advance copies of the author's book for class reading. Teacher to prepare pre-visit activities and follow-up writing assignment. Proposed dates within next six weeks; include estimated honorarium and travel needs.
personalized:
Hi Julia,

Exciting idea — would you be open to hosting a mystery-author visit for your fifth graders? I can reach out to a local writer who blends history with mystery and set up either a virtual Zoom session or an in-person visit (depending on the author's preference). My role: contact the author, coordinate tech or library space, collect student questions, and set aside five advance copies so classes can read beforehand (I can manage holds and checkouts). Could you lead pre-visit activities and a follow-up writing assignment that asks kids to try a historical mystery hook?

We should decide on a few date options within the next six weeks, confirm any honorarium or travel needs (I’ll draft a quick budget request for the PTA), and agree on the session format: 40-minute author talk plus 15 minutes for Q&A is my recommendation. I can also create a one-page prep sheet for students with suggested questions. What dates work for your class, and do you prefer in-person or virtual? I’ll start the inquiry and keep you posted.

Un abrazo, María

task_details: Second grade activity combining basic arithmetic and problem-solving within a scavenger hunt around the school. Objective is to practice addition/subtraction and positional words through clue-solving. Librarian to design eight math-clues, hide them in common areas, and create answer keys. Teacher to review safety, provide small teams, and incorporate reflection at the math block. Suggest schedule for a 30-minute hunt and 15-minute debrief. Provide materials list and permissions.
personalized:
Hola Rosa,

I'd love to co-create a math-and-mystery scavenger hunt for your second graders that gets them moving and practicing addition and subtraction through clues. I can design eight kid-friendly math clues, hide them in supervised common areas, and bring a simple answer key and reflection prompts for your math block. Let's aim for a 30-minute hunt and a 15-minute debrief where students explain how they solved each clue.

Practical items: we'll run teams of three, have two adult volunteers (do you have any classroom parents who can help?), and I’ll prepare laminated clue cards and a short route map. Teacher tasks would be reviewing safety and rules before we start, grouping kids, and leading the debrief. How does next Thursday morning sound? I can handle printing and circulation logistics (I’ll bring extra pencils), and I promise not to hide clues in the staff lounge (unless y'all want that extra mystery).

Qué opinas? María

Hi Sam,

Would you be interested in promoting a YA historical mystery book club for our seventh graders? I’ll curate three accessible titles that connect to the era you’re covering in social studies, create discussion guides, and host lunchtime meetings every other week for six weeks (I can reserve the library table). If you’d like to recommend students or co-facilitate a session, that would be wonderful; otherwise I’ll run it solo and send you brief updates so we can tie it to class content.

Plan: share a short sign-up sheet with students this week, I’ll order class sets or reserves as needed, and we’ll start in six weeks. I can provide snack ideas for meetings (kids love a cookie and a good mystery) and will prepare one quick writing prompt for each session. Want me to bring a themed display to catch students’ eyes? (I might add a knitted magnifying-glass cozy — just kidding, mostly.)

Gracias, María

Hola Elena,

Let’s do a makerspace day where first graders make detective notebooks to use during read-alouds and neighborhood walks. I’ll bring pre-cut notebook pages, stickers, crayons, yarn for binding, and a short template with sentence starters for observations. If you can pre-teach the vocabulary and help with transitions, I’ll model one page and run the table (I’ll take care of circulation the week we use the room).

Timing: a 30-minute makerspace session works best, with a few walking prompts for later observation practice. Materials note: safety scissors, glue sticks, and washable markers only. Do you have any students with sensory needs I should account for? I’ll prepare an alternative, low-stimulus kit. What day next week fits your schedule?

Abrazos, María

I’m putting in interlibrary loan requests for a class set of a procedural novel that pairs nicely with your science-methods unit for sixth grade. My plan is to stagger checkouts so groups read one section per week and complete a small project at the end.

Could you confirm the target weeks and whether you prefer rotating small groups or whole-class reads? I’ll handle holds and circulation logistics, and will include the ISBN when I submit the ILL. If the loan is delayed, I can make a digital packet with excerpts and scaffolded discussion questions. Want me to start the ILL request today?

Gracias, María

Let’s align on a shared rubric for inference, evidence use, and narrative-arc comprehension for your 4th and 5th graders. I’ll draft a practical rubric with anchor papers and suggested formative checkpoints we can use during library visits, and I can offer to run one-on-one conferences for students who need extra support (I can cover two afternoons of conferencing). Could you share any existing rubrics or sample student work so I match your standards exactly? I’ll have a draft ready in a week and we can meet to tweak it.

Suggested checkpoints: quick exit-ticket after a read-aloud, one small-group discussion observation, and a final written response. If we agree on scoring dates, I can help with clerical tasks like copying and uploading samples. Sound good? Want me to bring the draft to your planning period or email it first?

Un abrazo, María

task_instruction: Plan a bilingual family literacy night focused on mysteries for K-2 families
task_details: Organize a family literacy evening (bilingual Spanish-English) aimed at kindergarten through second grade, centered on mystery picture books, read-alouds, and simple clue games. Librarian to curate bilingual titles, set up reading corners, lead two short read-alouds, and provide activity stations. Teacher to promote the event to families and arrange childcare or translation support. Include timeline, materials, and volunteer needs.
personalized:
Hola Sara,

Would you be willing to co-host a bilingual family literacy night for our K–2 families focused on mysteries and read-aloud fun? I’ll curate bilingual mystery picture books, set up cozy reading corners, lead two short read-alouds (one in Spanish, one in English), and organize simple clue games families can play together. Could you promote the event on your class messaging platform and help recruit two volunteers for childcare at the door and translation support? I’ll provide a one-page flyer in both languages.

Tentative timeline: 6:00 welcome and snacks, 6:15 read-alouds, 6:30 activity stations, 7:00 closing. Materials I’ll handle: books, printables, and props. We’ll need two volunteers and a translator for announcements. Are you free to meet next week to finalize the flyer? I can bring coffee (and cookies) to the meeting.

Gracias, María

task_instruction: Propose a student mystery-writing contest and school zine
task_details: Launch a school-wide mystery-writing contest for grades 3-6 with a small zine publication combining student stories and illustrations. Librarian to manage submissions, editing workshops, and zine layout. Teachers to nominate students, run classroom writing time, and solicit illustrations. Timeline: submission window of three weeks, editing week, publication for school assembly. Include prizes and distribution plan.
personalized:
Hi Toni,

How about we run a school-wide mystery-writing contest for grades 3–6 and publish a small zine of the best stories and illustrations? I’ll manage submissions, host two lunchtime editing workshops, and handle layout and printing. If you can set aside a couple of classroom writing sessions and encourage students to submit, that would be perfect. We’ll keep the timeline tight: three-week submission window, one week of editing and layout, and a zine reveal at the assembly.

I’ll arrange small prizes (bookstore gift cards or donated titles) and a copy for every classroom. Could you nominate a few promising student writers and remind colleagues about the submission dates? I’ll draft submission guidelines and an editing checklist (I can run that first workshop during my prep). Want me to pop by your room to pitch it to students next week?

Abrazos, María

task_details: Create an in-class escape-room-style activity for third graders that reinforces a current science standard (e.g., plants or simple machines). Librarian to design puzzles, physical clues, and a scavenger hunt around the room; teacher to deliver science content and supervise puzzle stations. personalized:
Hola Marco,

I’ve been thinking about an escape-room-style activity that reinforces your third-grade science standard on simple machines. I can design age-appropriate puzzles and clues that require applying science concepts to solve them, hide clues around the room or library, and run the timed session. Would you lead the science mini-lesson beforehand and supervise one of the puzzle stations? I’ll provide a clear run sheet, safety rules, and differentiation options for different learners.

Proposed length: 45 minutes total with a 10-minute debrief on strategies used and vocabulary connections. Materials I’ll bring: laminated clue cards, timers, and small prizes. Do you have any concerns about space or timing next week? I can adapt puzzles for limited space if needed.

Qué te parece? María

task_instruction: Co-teach a media-literacy lesson on red herrings and inference for fifth graders
task_details: Fifth grade lesson exploring how authors and media use red herrings to mislead audiences, using short video clips, picture-book examples, and news literacy discussion. Librarian to provide curated clips and lead the red-herring activity; teacher to connect to writing standards and assign a short reflective paragraph. Plan for a 40-minute library session and a 20-minute classroom writing follow-up. Include assessment criteria and accommodations.
personalized:
Hi Laila,

Would you be open to a joint media-literacy and ELA lesson on red herrings and inference for your fifth graders? I’ll curate a few short, kid-appropriate video clips and picture-book examples that illustrate how authors and media plant misleading clues. In a 40-minute library session I’ll lead students in identifying red herrings and comparing intent across texts; could you assign a short reflective paragraph as a classroom follow-up and grade to your standards? I’ll provide an assessment checklist and accommodations for students who need it.

Logistics: I’ll handle tech setup and circulation, and suggest using a simple three-point rubric for the paragraph. Want me to email the clips and rubric in advance so you can preview them? (I always preview — habit of a librarian.)

Gracias, María

task_instruction: Propose a calming craft integration: knitting during independent reading time
task_details: Introduce an optional calming craft station (simple knitting/crochet or fidget knitting) during independent reading for upper elementary students to support focus and executive functioning. Librarian to supply materials, model techniques, and set usage guidelines. Teacher to recommend students who might benefit and monitor behavior. Clarify schedule, materials safety, and storage.
personalized:
Hola Debbie,

Quick thought: would you be open to piloting a calming craft station during independent reading for upper elementary students? I can bring simple knitting looms, yarn, and model one basic technique so students can quietly make a small bookmark while they read. The goal is to support focus and executive functioning for students who benefit from a hands-on anchor.

I’ll set clear usage guidelines, create a sign-out sheet, and store materials in a labeled bin. If you could recommend a few students who might benefit and help monitor behavior the first few sessions, that would be great. We’ll keep it optional and limited to a handful of students per session. Want to try this next Thursday during reading time? I’ll bring washable yarn and extra patience.

Abrazos, María

task_instruction: Request approval and funds for purchasing more mystery and procedural titles for the library
task_details: Prepare a brief request to the grade-level team lead asking for approval and funds (estimated amount) to purchase additional mystery and procedural titles for grades 3-6. Ask for PTA or discretionary funds and propose next steps.
personalized:
Hi Roberto,

I wanted to request approval for a modest purchase of mystery and procedural titles to better support our 3rd–6th grade curriculum. Circulation data shows strong demand for mysteries, and several of our upcoming units would benefit from more procedural models and mystery novels. I’ve put together a short wishlist of titles and an estimated cost of $450. My plan for new items: hold the set for classroom teachers during unit weeks and circulate them afterward (I’ll manage holds and checkout policy).

Would you be willing to sign off so I can submit a PTA funding request, or should I use discretionary funds? If helpful, I can present the wishlist and a quick justification at the next grade-level meeting. Let me know how you’d like to proceed and I’ll take care of the paperwork.

Gracias, María

task_instruction: Schedule a rotating read-aloud/book-talk visit for reluctant readers in second grade

Librarian to prepare a rotating set of 6-8 titles, lead 15-minute sessions with enthusiastic pitches, and set up a simple follow-up lending system. Teacher to identify students and provide a weekly time slot. Start within two weeks.
personalized:
Hola Brenda,

Would you be open to a rotating weekly 15-minute book-talk visit to your second-grade class to reach reluctant readers? I’ll bring a curated set of 6–8 high-interest picture and beginning-chapter books and do a lively pitch each week with a quick read-aloud hook. I’ll also set up a follow-up lending system so kids can check the titles immediately (I’ll manage circulation and holds).

If you can give me a weekly slot and identify a few students to focus on, I’ll get started in two weeks. My pitch will be short, friendly, and include a question to invite each child to check a book out. Want to try Thursday mornings at 9:00? I’ll bring a little prop for drama — no glitter, promise.

Abrazos, María

Let’s design a unit that pairs your local-history standards with historical-fiction mysteries for sixth graders. Gracias, María

The plan: 30-minute visits in small groups, with a short student reflection afterward. I’ll prepare an easy rubric for oral storytelling and a thank-you note template for volunteers. Want to try a pilot with your class next month? I promise lively conversations and maybe some old-school sleuthing tips.

Gracias, María

Want me to draft a permission slip and mentor contract? I can bring sign-up sheets to the staff meeting.

Gracias, María

Gracias, María

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, approachable and quietly authoritative — the voice of a caring teacher-librarian who enjoys friendly literary debate. Moderately formal in professional contexts but conversational and wry with colleagues and community members; shares clear, actionable recommendations and personal anecdotes to build rapport.
general_writing_style.syntax: Prefers clear declarative and compound sentences with occasional subordinate clauses for nuance; uses brief parenthetical asides and commas for friendly asides. Often poses rhetorical questions to engage readers and strings short clauses for checklist-style recommendations rather than long, ornate sentences.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Draws on library and literary vocabulary: words like 'catalog', 'circulation', 'hold request', 'interlibrary loan', 'ISBN', and genre labels such as 'cozy mystery', 'procedural', 'red herring' and 'narrative arc'. Also uses hobby-specific terms ('row', 'purl', 'cast on'; baking terms like 'proof', 'crumb', 'glaze'), everyday US measurements ('cups', 'degrees F'), and occasional Spanish phrases for warmth (e.g., '¿qué tal?', 'mi gente', '¡qué buen giro!').
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of contractions ('I'm', 'can't', 'we'll') and parenthetical asides ('(I time my knitting to scene breaks)'). Habitually invites participation with phrases and questions like 'Have you read...?', 'check it out', 'hold a copy', and uses community-oriented 'we' plus occasional regional or Spanish interjections such as 'y'all', 'oye' and 'claro'.

task_instruction: Submit FY2026 operating budget summary for board approval
task_details: Provide a concise operating budget summary for fiscal year 2026 with total amount requested and key line-item allocations (materials, staffing, utilities, programming, contingency). Attach the detailed spreadsheet. Request a vote at the next board meeting.
personalized:
Dear Members of the Library Board,

Please find attached the FY2026 operating budget summary for your review. The total appropriation requested is $1,200,000. Key line item allocations are as follows: materials $120,000 to maintain current collection turnover and expand digital resources; staffing $750,000 to sustain current hours and meet contractual obligations; utilities $80,000 reflecting modest projected increases; programming $50,000 to support youth and community outreach; contingency $50,000 for unforeseen expenses. The detailed spreadsheet with line-by-line figures and assumptions is attached for your records.

I recommend approval of the FY2026 operating budget as presented. Action requested: vote at the next regular board meeting to adopt the budget for the fiscal year beginning July 1. If you would like a brief walk-through of any line item before the meeting, I am happy to schedule time.

Thank you for your attention and support.

Sincerely,
María López, M.S. in Library and Information Science
Library Director (Interim)

task_instruction: Request reallocation within current fiscal year budget to fund summer reading
task_details: Ask the board to approve reallocating $15,000 from the office supplies line item to children's programming to expand the summer reading program. Explain justification, anticipated outcomes, and action requested (vote). Attach revised budget excerpt.
personalized:
Dear Board Chair and Members,

Please find attached a revised budget excerpt reflecting a proposed intra-fund reallocation for the current fiscal year. Due to increased community demand and participation projections for our summer reading program, I recommend transferring $15,000 from the office supplies line item to children's programming. This reallocation will fund additional materials, performer stipends, and outreach to Title I schools, which we anticipate will increase youth participation by at least 20 percent.

I recommend approval of this reallocation. Action requested: approval by majority vote at the upcoming meeting so we may execute contracts and place orders in time for program launch. I can provide attendance projections and vendor estimates upon request.

Warm regards,
María López
Elementary School Librarian

task_details: Request board approval to purchase an RFID circulation system at a cost of $48,000, to be funded from the building reserve fund. Include benefits (faster checkouts, inventory accuracy) and action requested: authorize purchase order.
personalized:
Dear Board Members,

Best,
María López

Sincerely,

María López

María López

task_details: Ask board to approve purchase of eight public computers at $900 each ($7,200 total) from the technology budget to replace aging machines. Provide justification and request authorization to execute purchase order.
personalized:
Dear Board Chair and Members,

Please find attached vendor quotes for eight new public access computers. The machines will replace end-of-life units and improve patron experience for job searches and homework help. The total cost is $7,200 (eight units at $900 each), to be paid from the technology line.

I recommend approval to purchase the computers and authorization to issue a purchase order so installations may be scheduled during the next maintenance window. Action requested: board approval at the upcoming meeting.

Best regards,
María López

Dear Members of the Board,

Please find attached circulation and program metrics for the past three years. These show steady growth in physical and digital circulation, increased program attendance, and higher hold request rates. To meet demand and reduce wait times, I propose a 5 percent increase to the materials budget in FY2027.

Action requested: review the attached data, provide feedback, and consider a vote to include the 5 percent increase in the FY2027 budget planning assumptions. I am prepared to present the metrics and expected outcomes in the next meeting.

Sincerely,
María López

Gracias,
María López

Dear Board Chair and Members,

Please find attached the donor's offer and shelving specifications. A local business has offered to donate three shelving units to expand our children’s area. While the donation is generous, there will be installation and freight expenses estimated at $1,500.

Action requested: approval to accept the in-kind donation and authorize up to $1,500 from the facilities line to cover installation. Accepting the shelves will immediately increase shelving capacity for youth materials, and I propose we acknowledge the donor in our newsletter.

Warmly,
María López

Please find attached the grant notice for the state construction program and preliminary project scope. The project would fund upgraded shelving and ADA access improvements to our main entrance. Sincerely,
María López

Please find attached a brief pilot plan for a weekend storytime aimed at working families who cannot attend weekday sessions. The pilot requires a one-time allocation of $1,200 to cover a youth librarian stipend and supplies for a three-month trial.

Gracias,
María López

Sincerely,
María López

task_details: Remind members about the next meeting on Thursday, May 12 at 6:30 PM in the community room at Oak Grove Library. personalized: Hola mi gente — quick reminder that we meet Thursday, May 12 at 6:30 PM in the community room at Oak Grove Library. We’ll be discussing The Hound of the Baskervilles by Arthur Conan Doyle. Have you savored the fog and moor yet? Bring a favorite line if one snagged you (I always underline the narrator’s asides). We’ll talk atmosphere and how the setting becomes almost a character, the use of deduction versus intuition, and any red herrings that sent you down the wrong path. I’ll bring cookies (glaze included). Can you reply and let me know if you’re coming so I can bake accordingly? See you soon — and yes, bring your copy so we can mark pages together.

Choose one scene you’d like to read aloud, maybe something that highlights pacing or a moral question. Bring thoughts and a pencil for margin notes (you know I will).

task_instruction: Welcome new members with an introduction to the club, meeting logistics, and participation expectations.
task_details: Write a warm welcome email for new members joining the community book club. Explain monthly meeting cadence (second Thursday at 6:30 PM), location (Oak Grove Library community room), how to check out copies through library circulation, how to request holds and interlibrary loan, expectations about participation, and mention optional knitting circle that meets during the first half hour. Invite them to share reading preferences and any accessibility needs.
personalized: Bienvenidos and welcome to our book club — so glad you joined us. We meet the second Thursday of every month at 6:30 PM in the Oak Grove Library community room, and we keep a calm, conversational pace. Library copies are available through circulation; if a copy is checked out you can place a hold request or ask me about interlibrary loan. We like lively but respectful conversation, and we encourage everyone to bring thoughts rather than polished essays. If you want to stitch while we chat, we have an optional knitting circle that gathers the first half hour — needles and kibitzing encouraged. Tell me a bit about your favorite genres and any accessibility needs so we can make meetings comfortable. I’ll be here to help you get your first copy on hold. ¿Qué tal?

task_instruction: Write an author spotlight email highlighting a classic mystery author and suggesting related titles to read next.
task_details: Spotlight Agatha Christie as inspiration. Summarize her style and mention three suggested reads for the group: Murder on the Orient Express, And Then There Were None, and The Murder of Roger Ackroyd. Offer to place interlibrary loan requests if members want hard-to-find editions and include an ISBN for a recommended edition of Murder on the Orient Express: 9780062693662. Invite thoughts on Christie’s influence at the next meeting on August 14 at 6:30 PM.
personalized: Hello detectives — quick author spotlight for your reading lists. Agatha Christie is the queen of the craft when it comes to tidy motives, clever red herrings, and those neat narrative reveals that make you say ¡qué buen giro! If you want to sample, try Murder on the Orient Express, And Then There Were None, or The Murder of Roger Ackroyd. If you want a specific edition, I can request Murder on the Orient Express ISBN 9780062693662 through interlibrary loan (let me know). We’ll weave Christie’s influence into our conversation on August 14 at 6:30 PM. Have you noticed her fingerprints on modern procedurals? Bring examples.

task_instruction: Send a meeting follow-up email recapping discussion highlights and listing action items.
task_details: After Monday's meeting on The Hound of the Baskervilles, send a recap that notes key points raised about setting, Holmes-Watson dynamic, and the use of unreliable narration. Action items: please vote on next month’s pick (I’ll send the options later this week), sign up if you want to bring snacks (we’re down to cookie volunteers), and post any favorite quotes to our group thread so we can compile them. Mark your calendars for our next meeting on September 9 at 6:30 PM. I’ll bring extra cookies and my knitting — quien se anima?

task_instruction: Circulation troubleshooting and common issues
task_details: List steps for resolving login failures, scanner jams, barcode misreads, and printer issues; include where extra supplies are and how to record persistent errors.

Printer: if prints queue, open the print dialog and cancel the stuck job, then restart the printer (spare toner in the cabinet). Supplies: extra barcode stickers and receipt paper in the lower cabinet labeled SUPPLIES. Record any persistent error in the tech log (brown binder by the phone) with time and a short note—I’ll submit an IT ticket tomorrow. You’ll do great — call/text (916) 555-0123 if something is urgent. Saludos, María

task_instruction: Behavior management and classroom visit guidance

personalized: Hi — behavior notes for the day (calm steps work best). Use a quiet, firm voice and offer choices (‘‘You can read here, or you can return the book to the shelf’’). For repeated disruptions, send a quick note to the teacher (do not leave the desk unattended) or call the classroom extension (numbers on the phone strip). During scheduled classroom visits, bring only the preselected books (list in the folder) and keep reading time to 20 minutes (teachers appreciate punctuality). If a child becomes upset, step to a quieter corner and offer a calming activity (coloring sheet in drawer). For anything beyond that, call the office or contact me at (916) 555-0123. You’ll do great — gracias, María

persona.brief_background: María structures her evenings around winding down with a well-crafted mystery or procedural — she times her knitting rows to scene breaks and often annotates plot points in the margins of her reading journal. She prioritizes community involvement (runs a weekly book club at the local library) and uses crime shows as a social bridge, recommending series to colleagues and bringing plot discussions into classroom reading activities.
persona.interests_lifestyle: watching mystery and crime TV series, true-crime and investigative podcasts, reading crime and historical fiction, community book club organizer, knitting, crossword puzzles, weekend baking, neighborhood volunteer storytime, streaming platform binging, occasional escape room outings

general_writing_style.tone: Warm, approachable and quietly authoritative — the voice of a caring teacher-librarian who enjoys friendly literary debate. Moderately formal in professional contexts but conversational and wry with colleagues and community members; shares clear, actionable recommendations and personal anecdotes to build rapport.
general_writing_style.syntax: Prefers clear declarative and compound sentences with occasional subordinate clauses for nuance; uses brief parenthetical asides and commas for friendly asides. Often poses rhetorical questions to engage readers and strings short clauses for checklist-style recommendations rather than long, ornate sentences.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Draws on library and literary vocabulary: words like 'catalog', 'circulation', 'hold request', 'interlibrary loan', 'ISBN', and genre labels such as 'cozy mystery', 'procedural', 'red herring' and 'narrative arc'. Also uses hobby-specific terms ('row', 'purl', 'cast on'; baking terms like 'proof', 'crumb', 'glaze'), everyday US measurements ('cups', 'degrees F'), and occasional Spanish phrases for warmth (e.g., '¿qué tal?', 'mi gente', '¡qué buen giro!').
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of contractions ('I'm', 'can't', 'we'll') and parenthetical asides ('(I time my knitting to scene breaks)'). Habitually invites participation with phrases and questions like 'Have you read...?', 'check it out', 'hold a copy', and uses community-oriented 'we' plus occasional regional or Spanish interjections such as 'y'all', 'oye' and 'claro'.

task_instruction: AV equipment setup for a classroom video session
task_details: Provide steps to set up projector and speakers, where the remote and cables are, how to connect a laptop, volume guidelines, and where to put equipment after use.
personalized: Hola — AV setup for today’s video lesson (short checklist). Projector: power on with the remote (on the cork tray). Connect the laptop via HDMI cable (long cable in the drawer). Speakers: small speaker on the shelf; plug into the audio jack and set volume to 30% (we keep it low to avoid hallway distraction). Test play a short clip before class starts. After use: shut down projector, coil cables, and return remotes to the cork tray. If the projector lamp is dim or shows an error, put a note in the tech log and place the projector cover back on. You’ll do great — call/text if the connection is wonky (916) 555-0123). Saludos, María

task_instruction: Book repair basics for common wear-and-tear
task_details: Give instructions on how to perform basic book repairs (torn pages, loose covers), where the repair kit is, and when to set aside for professional repair.
personalized: Hi — basic book repair guide (easy fixes). For torn pages, use acid-free tape from the repair kit (top drawer) and press flat for a minute. For loose covers, use the book repair glue and cloth tape (in the kit) to reattach and let dry under a heavy book for 30 minutes. For spine damage or severe mildew, set the book aside in the REPAIR shelf and fill out a Repair Request form (in the binder). Keep repairs simple—don’t attempt large restorations. Return the repair kit to the drawer when done. You’ll do great — text if you’re unsure about a repair (916) 555-0123). Gracias, María

task_instruction: Managing returns during a busy recess period
task_details: Explain efficient handling of returns when multiple classes come in: prioritizing check-ins, temporary shelving, quiet signposting, and notifying teachers of long lines.
personalized: Good morning — busy return protocol (keep it moving). When multiple classes arrive, set up a temporary returns bin (large tote by the door) and scan items as quickly as possible (students may help by holding books). If a line forms, place a 'Returns Here' sign (on the clipboard) so students know where to stand. Prioritize check-ins for teachers collecting items and then process student returns. If wait times exceed five minutes, notify the teacher via a quick hallway note so they can help manage the line. After the rush, sort returns and reshelve or place on the RESHELVES cart. You’ll do great — text if it becomes chaotic (916) 555-0123). Saludos, María

task_instruction: Managing the library budget petty cash and purchase requests
task_details: Explain how to document petty cash usage, where receipts go, and how to record teacher purchase requests for new titles.
personalized: Hi — petty cash and purchase request steps (short and clear). If you need petty cash for small supplies (under $10), take from the lockbox and write a receipt with the amount, purpose, and your initials (receipt book in the drawer). Return any unused change and attach receipts to the log sheet in the cash binder. For teacher purchase requests for new books, have them fill out a Purchase Request form (on the clipboard) with ISBN and justification. Place completed forms in the PURCHASES folder for me to review. You’ll do great — text if you need cash or forms (916) 555-0123). Gracias, María

task_instruction: Organizing a pop-up literacy event with parents
task_details: Provide instructions for a short parent-child literacy night: setup, guest flow, takeaways, sign-in, and cleanup.
personalized: Good afternoon — parent literacy pop-up notes (simple plan). Setup: arrange chairs in a semicircle and place a display table with handouts (handouts in the blue tote). Sign-in: parents sign the guest sheet at the door (clipboard on the counter). Flow: welcome families, read a short picture book, and offer a list of take-home activities (also on the table). Hand out literacy tip sheets and a bookmark to each child (bookmarks in the small box). Cleanup: fold chairs, stack handouts, and return leftover bookmarks to the supply drawer. If attendance is high, let the front desk know so they can assist. You’ll do great — text me if something comes up (916) 555-0123). Saludos, María

task_instruction: Implementing a short reader recommendation campaign
task_details: Explain how to collect staff and student recommendations, where to place recommendation cards, writing sample blurbs, and creating a small display.
personalized: Hi — reader recommendation campaign for the week (fun and easy). Place recommendation cards on the table (cards in the drawer) and invite students and staff to write a one-line blurb about a favorite book. Collect completed cards in the red box and pin them to the recommendation board (by the door). Create a small face-out display with the most popular picks and add a sign that says STAFF & STUDENT PICKS. If you want, write a short blurb yourself for the board (I always add a knitting-related note). Rotate the display midweek. You’ll do great — text me a photo if you want feedback (916) 555-0123). Gracias, María

task_instruction: Supporting classroom research with library resources
task_details: Provide a workflow for a short research support session: identify topic, pull age-appropriate resources, show students how to use the catalog, and leave follow-up materials for the teacher.
personalized: Good morning — research support steps for today’s third-grade class (20 minutes). Start by confirming the topic (topic note is in the folder). You’ll do great — text if you need more resources (916) 555-0123). Saludos, María

task_instruction: Volunteer-led reading buddy setup and rules
task_details: Explain pairing volunteers with students for reading buddies, rules for sessions, book selection limits, and clipboard documentation.
personalized: Hola — reading buddy program notes (simple supervision). Pair volunteers with students based on the buddy chart (in the folder). Volunteers should encourage reading for 20 minutes and keep interactions positive (no personal questions). Book selection: limit to one picture book or one early-chapter book per session (books on the buddy cart). Volunteers must stay within sight of staff and sign the session on the clipboard when finished. If a volunteer reports behavioral concerns, note it on the session sheet and inform the teacher. You’ll do great supervising—text if a volunteer is late or absent (916) 555-0123). Gracias, María

task_instruction: Managing donations and used book intake
task_details: Provide instructions for accepting book donations, sorting standards, where to put accepted and rejected books, and how to inform donors about policies.
personalized: Hi — donation intake process (keeps the stacks healthy). Accept donations at the counter and ask donors to sign the Donation Log (on the clipboard). Sort donations: accept clean, non-yellowed copies that fit our curriculum or student interest; recycle or rehome worn, outdated, or adult-only titles. Accepted books go on the DONATION PROCESS cart (for labeling), rejected books go in the RECYCLING box. If a donor asks for a receipt, provide the generic acknowledgement form (in the drawer) but not a tax valuation. Thank the donor warmly and let them know accepted books may go into circulation. You’ll do great — text if you’re unsure about a title (916) 555-0123). Saludos, María

task_instruction: Recommend a cozy mystery series appropriate for upper elementary readers.
task_details: Write an informal email to a fellow elementary teacher recommending a cozy mystery series suitable for grades 4-5. Explain why it fits that age group, suggest tie-in activities for reading groups, and note any content concerns. Keep tone friendly and include a brief personal anecdote to build rapport.
personalized:
Hi Ana —

Have you read the Hazel Wong mysteries (Angela Misri)? They're a cozy mystery series that lands nicely for our fourth and fifth graders: age-appropriate sleuthing, lots of clever clues, and a main character who models curiosity and persistence. I put the first two on hold and used them for a small guided reading group last month (the kids loved the detective gadgets and kept calling me to say 'look what I noticed!').

For tie-ins, try a clue-mapping activity and a vocabulary scavenger hunt—both low-prep and great for cross-group discussion. Only heads-up: there's light peril and mild references to family tensions, so I'd pre-read if you're particularly cautious about content, but nothing graphic. Want me to hold a class set put on the cart? Thoughts?

task_instruction: Suggest a procedural TV series colleagues can stream for a staff movie night.
task_details: Email a colleague recommending a TV procedural that's office-friendly for a staff streaming night. Mention episode length, why it's fun for fans of mysteries, any streaming platform info, and a playful anecdote connecting it to school life. Keep tone conversational and enthusiastic.
personalized:
Oye Marco —

Staff night — procedural edition? I vote for Brooklyn Nine-Nine (yes, it's more police-comedy than heavy procedural, but perfect if we want laughs and clever mysteries that wrap up in 20 minutes). Episodes are short, so we can binge-watch a few without committing a whole evening. It's great for folks who like neat mystery arcs and quick red herrings (and trust me, the characters keep things light when the plot gets twisty).

It's on Peacock/Netflix depending on your account (I'll double-check). Want me to bring cookies? I can time my knitting to commercial breaks (I timed my knitting to the season finale last month). ¿Qué tal?

task_instruction: Recommend a middle-grade mystery series for reluctant readers.
task_details: Compose an email to a colleague suggesting a middle-grade mystery series that appeals to reluctant readers. Mention pacing, language level, how to introduce it in the library, and a simple strategy to hook shy readers. Keep it warm and practical.
personalized:
Hi Sam —

For our reluctant readers, try The Mysterious Benedict Society. Short chapters, quirky characters, and puzzles that pull kids in without heavy text. I shelf it right at eye-level and label it 'If you like puzzles'—that little nudge helps more than you'd think.

Hook strategy: read the first page aloud during check-out and hand the book to anyone who glances over. Works like a charm (I've converted a steady stream of 'I don't read' fifth graders). Want me to make a quick display and add a 'Try a Page' sticky note?

Hola Rosa —

I'd love to run a 45-minute Mystery Storytime for K-2: read a short cozy mystery picture book, do a simple 'Who took the cookie?' clue trail (with picture clues), and finish with a 'solve the mystery' circle where kids share ideas. Materials: one picture book, printed picture-clues, stickers for finding clues, and a small prize (sticker or bookmark). We can run it on a Tuesday afternoon after school—I'll handle props if you can spare a volunteer.

No real safety issues (all pretend), but we'll send a quick permission blurb to parents about snacks and photos. Want me to draft the flyer?

personalized:
Hola Jorge —

For our adult book club night, consider the 'The Teacher's Pet' episode from Casefile (or the investigative series version). It's rich in narrative arc and raises great questions about sources, bias, and community memory—perfect for a lively discussion. Heads-up: it deals with disturbing subject matter and includes mature themes, so warn attendees.

Warm-up questions: How did the narrative shape your sense of truth? What red herrings did you notice? I listened on my morning walk (podcast plus brisk steps equals focus) and I'd be happy to lead the conversation if you want. Thoughts?

Hola Luz —

Have you checked out La Familia Centenario's mystery picture books (or try bilingual editions like Enola Holmes bilingual adaptations)? There's also La Detective de la Abuela for younger readers—simple language, cultural touchstones, and a proud Mexican-American viewpoint that our bilingual kiddos will recognize. Great for language support and representation.

Class activity: bilingual suspect bulletin board where kids post clues in Spanish or English. For parent engagement, offer a short evening reading in español and send home bilingual reading tips. I can pull a few titles and bring them to your classroom for you to preview. ¿Te late?

task_instruction: Recommend a middle school mystery writing workshop outline for students.

Hi Daniel —

I'd like to run a three-session Mystery Writing Workshop for our 6th–8th graders: session one on plotting and motivates, session two on planting clues and red herrings (practice exercise), and session three on revision and peer critique. Materials: guided worksheets, index cards for clue-mapping, and a checklist for pacing. Outcomes: a one-chapter mystery draft and peer feedback; assessment can be a rubric based on plot coherence and clue placement.

Happy to co-teach or lead—I'd love your input on timing. Shall we try next month after school?

task_instruction: Recommend graphic novel mysteries for visually-oriented readers.
task_details: Compose an email to a colleague recommending three graphic novel mystery titles suitable for upper elementary and middle school. Briefly explain why each works for visual learners and how to feature them for reluctant readers. Keep tone light and persuasive.
personalized:
Hey Toni —

For visually-minded kids, try Ghosts of Michigan, The Nameless City Mysteries, and Jedi Academy-style mystery graphic novels (think short, punchy panels). Graphic formats break text into manageable chunks and the art helps infer motives and clues—perfect for readers who shy away from chapter books. I shelved a few near our nonfiction comics and they flew off the cart.

Want me to set up a 'Graphic Mystery' mini-display? I can add a 'Try This If' note for reluctant readers.

task_instruction: Advise on ordering classroom sets and placing holds for a new mystery series.
task_details: Write an email to a teacher explaining the process to order a classroom set or place library holds/interlibrary loan for a new mystery series. Include steps, timeline, cost considerations, and offer to coordinate. Keep tone helpful and organized with a friendly touch.
personalized:
Hola Elena —

If you want a classroom set of the Owl Hollow mysteries, I can coordinate a hold request and price out a classroom purchase. Steps: tell me how many copies you need and your preferred format, I'll check our catalog and local vendors, and if out of budget I'll place interlibrary loan requests (those take longer—usually two weeks). Cost-wise, paperbacks are cheaper; library bindings cost more but last longer.

Tell me numbers and timeline and I'll get quotes. Always happy to split the work—I like cataloging adventures almost as much as a good whodunit (almost).
